title: Attention and the Transformer
summary: Why recurrence limited sequence models, how scaled dot-product attention mixes token vectors, and how masks, heads, positional encodings and residual blocks make up the Transformer.
outcomes: Explain why RNN encoder-decoders were hard to parallelize and how attention shortens the path between distant tokens
Compute scaled dot-product attention by hand for a few tokens, including the causal mask
Explain why scores are divided by the square root of d_k and what multi-head attention buys
Describe every part of a Transformer layer: positional encoding, attention, FFN, residuals and LayerNorm
Estimate where attention's quadratic cost dominates and explain post-LN vs pre-LN and decoder-only variants

lessons.title: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models

blocks.md:
In 2017 the best systems for **sequence transduction** (turning one sequence into another, such as translating English to German) were recurrent neural networks (RNNs), usually LSTMs or GRUs, arranged as an **encoder** that reads the source and a **decoder** that writes the target.

An RNN computes a hidden state $h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$: the state at position $t$ needs the state at $t-1$. You already know how tokens become embedding vectors $x_t$; the question here is how to mix information *between* those vectors.

That recurrence causes three problems:

1. **No parallelism inside a sequence.** Position 50 cannot start until position 49 is done, so a GPU sits mostly idle on long inputs.
2. **Long paths.** Information from token 1 must pass through every intermediate state to reach token 50, and long paths make long-range dependencies harder to learn.
3. **A fixed-size bottleneck.** In the basic encoder-decoder, the whole source sentence is squeezed into one fixed-length vector before decoding starts.

blocks.title: From a fixed vector to attention over every state

scenes.caption: An RNN encoder reads one token at a time. Each hidden state h depends on the previous one, so the four states are computed strictly in order.
Basic encoder-decoder: only the last state becomes the fixed vector c that the decoder sees. A 4-word and a 40-word sentence get the same number of numbers.
Path length: a signal from 'the' must cross h1, h2, h3 and h4 before it reaches c. The longer the sentence, the longer this path.
Bahdanau et al. (2014): at every decoder step, score all encoder states and take a weighted sum. The decoder now looks back at every word directly instead of through c.
The remaining problem is the h1 to h4 chain itself: it is still sequential. The Transformer (2017) removes it and lets every position attend to every other position in one step.

blocks.md:
Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio called the fixed-length vector "a bottleneck" and let the decoder *(soft-)search* the source: for each output word it computes a score for every encoder state, turns the scores into weights that sum to 1, and uses the weighted sum. That is **attention**.

Attention was still bolted onto an RNN. Vaswani et al. asked what happens if attention is the *only* way positions exchange information. Their model, the **Transformer**, "dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely".

blocks.title: Sequential steps: one RNN layer vs one self-attention layer

scenes.caption: Simplified model: one time unit per dependent step. An RNN layer over 6 tokens needs 6 steps, each waiting for the last.
A self-attention layer computes all 6 outputs from matrix products that do not depend on each other, so the number of sequential steps does not grow with length.
The catch: attention compares every pair of positions (36 here), so its work grows with n squared, but it is work a GPU can run in parallel. Lesson 5 returns to that cost.

blocks.tex: \begin{array}{lccc} \text{layer} & \text{work per layer} & \text{sequential ops} & \text{max path} \\ \text{self-attention} & O(n^2 d) & O(1) & O(1) \\ \text{recurrent} & O(n d^2) & O(n) & O(n) \end{array}
blocks.caption: From Table 1 of Attention Is All You Need. n is sequence length, d is the representation size.

blocks.prompt: A sentence has 50 tokens. How many dependent (sequential) steps does one RNN layer need, and how many does one self-attention layer need? How many steps does a signal cross to get from token 1 to token 50 in each?
blocks.reveal: The RNN layer needs **50** sequential steps and a signal from token 1 crosses up to **49** recurrent transitions to reach token 50. A self-attention layer needs a **constant** number of sequential steps (a few matrix multiplications), and token 50 reads token 1 **directly** in one layer. That is the *max path length* column: $O(n)$ vs $O(1)$.

blocks.md: The Transformer's core bet: replace the recurrent chain with attention, so every position can read every other position in one layer and the whole layer runs as parallel matrix multiplications.
Attention did not start with the Transformer. Additive attention over RNN states dates to Bahdanau et al. (2014). What was new in 2017 was using attention *alone*, with no recurrence or convolution.

blocks.question: Which problem of the basic RNN encoder-decoder did Bahdanau-style attention fix, and which did it leave in place?
options: It fixed sequential computation but kept the fixed-length vector
It removed the fixed-length vector bottleneck but kept the sequential recurrent chain
It fixed both, which is why the Transformer only changed the training recipe
It fixed neither; it only made the model more interpretable
blocks.explain: The decoder could now look at every encoder state through a weighted sum, so the single fixed vector stopped being a bottleneck. The encoder and decoder were still RNNs, so computation inside a sequence stayed sequential. The Transformer removed that remaining chain.

blocks.question: Per Table 1 of the paper, for which sequences is one self-attention layer cheaper in total work than one recurrent layer?
options: Always, because it has O(1) sequential operations
When the sequence length n is larger than the model width d
When n is smaller than d, which is typical for sentence-length inputs
Never; it is only faster because of parallelism
blocks.explain: Self-attention costs about $n^2 d$ and a recurrent layer about $n d^2$, so attention does less total work when $n < d$. The paper notes this is usually the case for sentences with d = 512. Sequential operations are a separate column: they measure parallelism, not total work.

lessons.title: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens

blocks.md:
The paper defines attention as "mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output". Think of a soft dictionary lookup:

- the **query** $q$ says what this position is looking for,
- each **key** $k_j$ advertises what position $j$ contains,
- each **value** $v_j$ is what position $j$ hands over if selected.

The output is a weighted sum of the values, where the weight on $v_j$ comes from how well $q$ matches $k_j$. In **self-attention** all three come from the same sequence.

Each token embedding $x_i$ (a row of the matrix $X$) is projected three ways by learned matrices. We use a toy: 4 tokens, embeddings of size 3, and projections to size $d_k = 2$. The weights are small integers so you can check the arithmetic; real models learn them.

blocks.caption: Rows of X are the tokens the, cat, sat, down. Q = XW^Q, K = XW^K, V = XW^V.

blocks.title: Projecting four tokens into queries, keys and values

scenes.caption: Every token gets its own query, key and value. They are just X multiplied by three different learned matrices.
Example: sat has x = (1,1,1), so q = (1,1,1)W^Q = (1,1). The same row of X gives k = (-1,2) and v = (4,4).
To compute the output for sat, its query is compared with every key. The best match is cat's key (1,1): dot product 1x1 + 1x1 = 2.

blocks.caption: Equation 1 of the paper. Row i of QK^T holds query i dotted with every key; softmax is applied to each row.

blocks.title: Scores, scaling and softmax for the toy sentence

scenes.caption: Step 1: raw scores QK^T. Row = the query's token, column = the key's token. Row sat is (-1, 2, 1, 0): sat's query matches cat's key best.
Step 2: divide every score by the square root of d_k = 2 (about 1.41). The order inside each row is unchanged; only the spread shrinks.
Step 3: softmax each row so it is positive and sums to 1 (values rounded to 2 decimals). sat now puts weight 0.54 on cat, 0.27 on itself, 0.13 on down and 0.06 on the.
Every row is its own distribution. down splits its weight between the and sat (0.38 each); cat mostly reads itself (0.62).

blocks.title: One row of softmax for the query of sat

scenes.caption: Scaled scores for sat (rounded): -0.71, 1.41, 0.71, 0.00.
Exponentiate each score. Everything becomes positive and the gap widens; the sum is 7.63.
Divide by that sum. These are the attention weights of sat; they sum to 1.

blocks.caption: The output for sat is the weighted sum of all four value vectors. It is a new vector that blends what sat found relevant.

blocks.prompt: We divided the scores by the square root of d_k. If we had skipped that step for sat's row, would the weight on cat go up or down?
blocks.reveal: It goes **up**, from 0.54 to 0.64. Without scaling the raw scores (-1, 2, 1, 0) are more spread out, and softmax turns a larger spread into a sharper, more one-hot distribution. With $d_k = 2$ the effect is mild. With $d_k = 64$ it is severe, as the next figure shows.

blocks.md: Why divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$? The paper's footnote: if the components of $q$ and $k$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then $q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$ has mean 0 and **variance $d_k$**. A Monte Carlo check with 200,000 random pairs at $d_k = 64$ gives variance 63.8, so typical scores are about $\pm 8$. Large scores push softmax into a region where it is nearly one-hot and its gradients are tiny. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ brings the variance back to 1.

blocks.title: Softmax over 5 random keys at d_k = 64

scenes.caption: Unscaled: raw scores of one random query with 5 random keys (d_k = 64) are 1.0, -9.4, 7.5, -4.8, 2.5. Key 3 takes 0.992 of the weight and the softmax Jacobian (sum of absolute entries) is only 0.033: almost no gradient.
Softmax after dividing by 8 (the square root of 64): weights spread to 0.19, 0.05, 0.43, 0.09, 0.23 and the Jacobian total rises to 1.42, about 43 times larger.

blocks.md: Scaling by the square root of d_k is not mainly about float overflow (implementations subtract the row max before exponentiating anyway). It keeps softmax out of its saturated, near one-hot region so gradients stay usable as d_k grows.

Attention output for a position = softmax(its query dotted with every key, divided by the square root of d_k), used as weights on the value vectors. Every step is a matrix multiply or a row-wise softmax, so all positions are computed at once.

blocks.question: In the toy example, which statement about the attention weights of sat is correct?
options: sat attends most to itself because a token always matches its own key best
sat attends most to cat because q_sat dotted with k_cat = 2 is the largest score in its row
All four weights are equal because the values are different sizes
The weights depend on the value vectors
blocks.explain: Weights come only from query-key dot products: sat's row is (-1, 2, 1, 0) and the 2 belongs to cat. A token does not automatically match itself best, because W^Q and W^K are different matrices. Values only enter after the weights are fixed.

blocks.question: You double d_k from 64 to 128 but forget to change the scale factor (still dividing by 8). What happens to the attention weights at initialization?
options: Nothing; the scale factor only matters for d_k below 64
They become flatter, because more dimensions average out
They become negative for half the keys
They become sharper (closer to one-hot), because score variance doubled while the divisor stayed the same
blocks.explain: With unit-variance components, score variance equals d_k. At d_k = 128 the scaled scores have variance 128/64 = 2 instead of 1, so softmax is more peaked and gradients shrink. Dividing by the square root of 128 restores variance 1.

lessons.title: Causal masks, cross-attention and multiple heads

blocks.md:
A translation decoder produces the target one token at a time, and each prediction may use only earlier tokens. During training we feed the whole target sentence at once (shifted right by one position), so we must stop position $i$ from reading positions after $i$.

The paper does this inside the attention function: before softmax, scores for illegal connections are set to $-\infty$. Since $e^{-\infty} = 0$, those keys get exactly zero weight. Because the mask covers everything above the diagonal, it is called a **causal** (or look-ahead) mask.

blocks.title: Applying a causal mask to the toy attention weights

scenes.caption: Unmasked weights from the last lesson (rounded). The query of the also reads cat, sat and down, which all come later.
Mask every cell above the diagonal: its score becomes minus infinity before softmax, so it gets weight 0.
Softmax renormalizes over the allowed keys only. the can only read itself (1.00). cat now splits 0.11 / 0.89 between the and cat.
sat keeps the same ratios as before over the three allowed keys: 0.07, 0.62, 0.31. down, the last token, is unchanged.

blocks.prompt: Before looking at the last scene: does the causal mask change the weights of down, the last token?
blocks.reveal: No. down already comes after every other token, so nothing in its row is masked: its weights stay (0.38, 0.05, 0.38, 0.19). Masking only changes rows that had weight on later tokens, and each such row renormalizes over the keys that remain.

blocks.title: Masked attention in NumPy, step by step
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def softmax(s):
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def attention(Q, K, V, causal=False):
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)
    if causal:
        n = scores.shape[0]
        future = np.triu(np.ones((n, n)), k=1).astype(bool)
        scores = np.where(future, -np.inf, scores)
    weights = softmax(scores)
    return weights @ V, weights

Q = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1], [-1, 1]], float)
K = np.array([[-2, 1], [1, 1], [-1, 2], [-1, 1]], float)
V = np.array([[3, 4], [1, 0], [4, 4], [2, 2]], float)
out, w = attention(Q, K, V, causal=True)
print(np.round(w, 2))
print(np.round(out, 2))

scenes.caption: Q, K, V are the toy matrices from Lesson 2: 4 tokens, d_k = 2.
One matrix product computes all 16 query-key scores at once, then they are scaled.
np.triu with k=1 marks the cells strictly above the diagonal: the future.
Future scores become -inf. The softmax subtracts the row max first, which is safe because every row keeps its diagonal entry.
Weighted sum of values. Row 1 (cat) is 0.11 x (3,4) + 0.89 x (1,0).

blocks.md:
The Transformer uses the same attention function in **three places**:

1. **Encoder self-attention**: queries, keys and values all come from the previous encoder layer; no mask, every source position sees every other.
2. **Masked decoder self-attention**: the same, over the target tokens, with the causal mask.
3. **Encoder-decoder (cross) attention**: queries come from the decoder, keys and values come from the encoder output. This is the Bahdanau-style lookup from Lesson 1, rebuilt with dot products.

One attention function produces one weighted average per position, and averaging blurs things together. The fix is **multi-head attention**: run $h$ attention functions in parallel, each with its own smaller projections, then concatenate and project back.

The base model uses $d_{\text{model}} = 512$ and $h = 8$ heads, each with $d_k = d_v = 512/8 = 64$. Because each head is 8 times narrower, the total cost is similar to one full-width head.

blocks.caption: W_i^Q, W_i^K are 512 x 64, W_i^V is 512 x 64, and W^O is (8 x 64) x 512.

blocks.title: How 512 dimensions are split into 8 heads

scenes.caption: Each position starts as one 512-dimensional vector.
Eight separate learned projections map it to eight 64-dimensional queries (and keys and values). Each head computes its own attention pattern over the sequence.
The eight 64-dimensional outputs are concatenated back to 512 and mixed by W^O. 8 x 64 = 512, so the per-layer cost matches one 512-wide head.

blocks.title: Table 3 (A): changing the number of heads at fixed compute

scenes.caption: BLEU (n-gram overlap with reference translations, higher is better) on the English-German dev set for the base model, keeping h x d_k = 512. One head is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best.
Dev perplexity (lower is better) tells the same story: 8 or 16 heads are best, while 1 head and 32 tiny 16-dimensional heads both lose quality.

blocks.md: Multi-head attention = several narrow attention functions in parallel, each free to learn a different pattern, at roughly the cost of one wide head.

blocks.question: In encoder-decoder (cross) attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from?
options: Queries, keys and values all come from the encoder output
Queries from the encoder; keys and values from the decoder
Queries from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder output
Queries and keys from the decoder; values from the encoder
blocks.explain: The decoder is asking questions about the source, so it supplies the queries. The encoder output supplies the keys (what each source position offers) and the values (what gets copied). This lets every decoder position attend over all input positions.

blocks.question: A bug report: a decoder trains to near-zero loss quickly, but generates garbage at inference. Which bug is most likely?
options: The scale factor uses d_model instead of d_k
The causal mask is missing, so during training each position could read the token it was supposed to predict
The model uses 8 heads instead of 1
The softmax is applied over columns instead of rows
blocks.explain: With teacher forcing the whole target is fed in at once. Without the causal mask, position i can attend to position i+1 (its own answer), so training is trivially easy. At inference those future tokens do not exist yet, and the model has never learned to predict without them.

blocks.question: With d_model = 512, how many parameters are in the four projection matrices (W^Q, W^K, W^V for all heads, plus W^O) of one multi-head attention layer, ignoring biases?
blocks.explain: Each of W^Q, W^K, W^V is 8 heads x (512 x 64) = 512 x 512 in total, and W^O is 512 x 512. That gives 4 x 512^2 = 1,048,576 weights. Splitting into heads does not multiply the parameter count.

lessons.title: Positional encoding, residuals and the full Transformer

blocks.md:
Attention has a blind spot: it ignores order. Each output is a weighted sum where the weights depend only on query-key dot products, and nothing in that formula mentions where a token sits.

Formally, self-attention is **permutation equivariant**: shuffle the input rows and the output rows are shuffled the same way, with identical values.

blocks.prompt: Feed the toy sentence in reverse order (down, sat, cat, the) through the same attention layer with no positional information. What is the output vector for sat?
blocks.reveal: Exactly the same as before: (2.06, 1.58). Our script checks all four rows: reversing the input just reverses the output rows. To the layer, "the cat sat down" and "down sat cat the" are the same bag of tokens. Word order has to be injected separately.

blocks.md: The paper adds a **positional encoding** to each input embedding at the bottom of the encoder and decoder stacks. It has the same size $d_{\text{model}}$ so the two can simply be summed. Each pair of dimensions is a sine and cosine at its own frequency:

blocks.caption: pos is the token position and i indexes dimension pairs. Wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2 pi to 10000 x 2 pi.

blocks.title: One dimension pair of the sinusoidal encoding (d_model = 512)

scenes.caption: i = 0: the fastest pair, wavelength 6.3 positions. It distinguishes neighbors but repeats every few tokens.
i = 32: wavelength 19.9 positions.
i = 64: wavelength 62.8 positions. Slower pairs separate tokens that are far apart.
i = 128: wavelength 628 positions, nearly flat over 100 tokens. Together the 256 pairs give every position a distinct fingerprint, like the digits of a clock.

blocks.title: Encodings for positions 0 to 3 with d_model = 8

scenes.caption: A toy 8-dimensional encoding computed from the formula. Position 0 is (0,1) in every pair because sin 0 = 0 and cos 0 = 1.
Dimensions 0 and 1 (fastest pair) change a lot from one position to the next.
Dimensions 6 and 7 (slowest pair) barely move over 4 positions; they would only change over thousands of tokens.

blocks.md: The authors chose sinusoids because, for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$, which they hypothesized makes relative positions easy to learn, and because it might extrapolate to longer sequences. Learned position embeddings gave nearly identical results (Table 3 row E: 25.7 vs 25.8 BLEU).

Each layer wraps its sub-layers in two more pieces:

- A **position-wise feed-forward network (FFN)**, applied to each position separately: $\text{FFN}(x)=\max(0,\,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2$, with inner width $d_{ff} = 2048$. Attention mixes information *across* positions; the FFN transforms each position on its own.
- A **residual connection** plus **layer normalization** around every sub-layer. In the original paper the output is $\text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))$. LayerNorm rescales each position's vector to zero mean and unit variance, then applies a learned gain and bias.

scenes.caption: Encoder layer: self-attention, then add & norm, then the FFN, then add & norm. N = 6 identical layers (separate weights) are stacked, all of width 512.
The final encoder layer's output z is computed once per source sentence and reused by every decoder layer.
Decoder layer, sub-layer 1: masked self-attention over the target tokens so far (each sub-layer also has add & norm, omitted here for space).
Sub-layer 2: cross-attention. Queries come from the decoder, keys and values from z.
Sub-layer 3: FFN. After 6 decoder layers a linear layer plus softmax gives a probability for every vocabulary token. The paper shares this linear layer's weights with the embedding matrices.

blocks.md: Where do the parameters live? With $d_{\text{model}} = 512$, one attention sub-layer has $4 \times 512^2$ weights plus biases = 1,050,624. One FFN has $2 \times 512 \times 2048$ weights plus biases = 2,099,712. So about **two-thirds** of an encoder layer's parameters are in the FFN, not in attention. The paper reports 65 million parameters for the whole base model, which also multiplies its embeddings by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ and shares one matrix between the input embeddings and the output projection.

"Attention is all you need" does not mean attention is all there is. Without the FFN, residual connections, normalization and positional encodings, a stack of attention layers loses most of its parameters, its sense of order, and its trainability.
A Transformer layer = attention (mix across positions) + FFN (transform each position), each wrapped in a residual connection and LayerNorm, with positional information added once at the input.

blocks.question: You remove the positional encodings from a trained encoder and feed it "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". What happens to the encoder output for the token "man"?
options: It is identical in both sentences
It differs, because attention weights depend on which tokens are nearby
It differs, because the FFN processes positions in order
It becomes all zeros
blocks.explain: Without positional information, self-attention and the position-wise FFN are permutation equivariant. Both sentences contain the same three tokens, so "man" gets the same output in each. That is why order must be injected explicitly.

blocks.question: Which sub-layer holds the most parameters in one base-model encoder layer?
options: Multi-head self-attention, because it has 8 heads
LayerNorm, because it has a gain and bias per dimension
The position-wise feed-forward network, about twice as many as attention
They are equal by design
blocks.explain: Attention: 4 x 512^2, about 1.05 million. FFN: 2 x 512 x 2048, about 2.10 million. LayerNorm has only 2 x 512 = 1,024 per instance. Heads split the attention width; they do not add parameters.

lessons.title: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017

blocks.md:
The paper trained on WMT 2014 English-German (about 4.5 million sentence pairs, byte-pair vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens) on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model ran 100,000 steps in about 12 hours; the big model ($d_{\text{model}} = 1024$, 16 heads, 213 million parameters) ran 300,000 steps in 3.5 days and reached **28.4 BLEU** on English-German, more than 2 BLEU above previous results including ensembles.

The recipe: Adam with $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.98$, $\epsilon = 10^{-9}$; dropout 0.1 (0.3 for the big English-German model) on each sub-layer output and on the embedding sums; label smoothing 0.1; and a warmup learning-rate schedule:

blocks.caption: Linear increase for the first warmup steps, then decay proportional to the inverse square root of the step number.

blocks.title: The warmup schedule from the paper (d_model = 512)

scenes.caption: With warmup = 4000 the rate climbs linearly to a peak of 0.70e-3 at step 4000, then decays; by step 100,000 it is 0.14e-3.
Shorter warmup (1000 steps) gives a higher, earlier peak of 1.40e-3. The peak equals d_model^-0.5 x warmup^-0.5.
Longer warmup (10000) peaks lower, at 0.44e-3. After warmup all settings follow the same inverse square root curve.

blocks.md: Now the cost. Per layer, the score matrix $QK^\top$ and the weighted sum with $V$ each take about $n^2 d$ multiply-adds, so they grow **quadratically** with sequence length $n$. The projections ($4nd^2$) and the FFN ($2nd\,d_{ff} = 8nd^2$ when $d_{ff} = 4d$) grow only linearly in $n$. The $n \times n$ weight matrix also has to be stored per head.

blocks.prompt: For d = 512 and d_ff = 2048, at what sequence length does the quadratic attention part (2n^2 d) start to cost more than the projections plus FFN (12nd^2)?
blocks.reveal: Set $2n^2 d = 12 n d^2$, so $n = 6d = 3072$ tokens, where both cost about 9.7 billion multiply-adds per layer. At $n = 512$ the quadratic part is only 14% of the layer's matmul work; at $n = 32{,}768$ it is 91%. For sentence-length inputs the FFN dominates; for long contexts attention does.

blocks.title: Per-layer matmul cost vs sequence length (simplified)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: counts only matrix-multiply work in one layer, with d_ff = 4d; softmax, LayerNorm and memory traffic are ignored. At d = 512 the lines cross at n = 3072.
Wider models push the crossover out: at d = 2048 it is at n = 12,288. The quadratic term still wins eventually, which is why long-context work focuses on attention.

blocks.md:
Two changes since 2017 are worth knowing:

- **Where the LayerNorm goes.** The paper is *post-LN*: normalize after adding the residual. Xiong et al. (2020) showed that post-LN has large gradients near the output at initialization, which is why the warmup stage matters, and that *pre-LN* (normalize the sub-layer input, keep the residual path clean) trains well even without warmup. Jurafsky and Martin's textbook calls pre-norm the most common architecture today.
- **Which halves are kept.** Liu et al. (2018) introduced a **decoder-only** Transformer: drop the encoder and cross-attention, join input and output into one sequence with a separator token, and train it as a standard next-token language model. Encoder-only models with no causal mask are used for masked language modeling.

blocks.title: Post-LN (2017 paper) vs pre-LN residual block

scenes.caption: Post-LN, as in the paper: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The normalization sits on the main path, so every layer's output passes through it.
Pre-LN: x + Sublayer(LayerNorm(x)). LayerNorm moves to the sub-layer's input, leaving an un-normalized residual path from bottom to top (a final LayerNorm is added after the last layer).
The residual edge now carries x straight to the output. Xiong et al. found this keeps gradients well-behaved at initialization, so the warmup stage can be dropped.

blocks.md: "Transformer" does not mean "GPT". The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder for translation. Decoder-only language models keep only its masked self-attention stack; encoder-only models keep only the unmasked encoder.
Attention trades sequential steps for quadratic pairwise work. That is a great deal on GPUs for moderate n, and the reason long-context methods all target the n x n score matrix.

blocks.question: A team switches a 24-layer post-LN Transformer to pre-LN. According to Xiong et al. (2020), what change to the training recipe becomes reasonable to try?
options: Removing or shortening the learning-rate warmup stage
Removing the causal mask
Dividing by d_k instead of its square root
Removing positional encodings
blocks.explain: Xiong et al. show that post-LN has large expected gradients near the output at initialization, which makes warmup necessary. With LayerNorm inside the residual branch (pre-LN) the gradients are well-behaved and they train without warmup at comparable quality.

blocks.question: You increase the context length of a model from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens and keep d fixed. Roughly how does the score-matrix work per layer change?
options: It grows about 4 times, like the FFN
It grows about 16 times, while the FFN work grows about 4 times
It stays the same because heads run in parallel
It grows about 2 times
blocks.explain: Score work scales with n^2: (16384/4096)^2 = 16. The FFN and projections scale with n, so they grow 4 times. Parallel heads change wall-clock time, not the amount of work.

blocks.question: Which statement about the paper's learning-rate schedule is correct?
options: It starts at its maximum and decays linearly to zero
It is constant at 1e-3 because Adam adapts the rate per parameter
It increases linearly for 4000 steps, then decays with the inverse square root of the step
It increases for the whole run
blocks.explain: Equation 3 is the minimum of a linear ramp and an inverse square root curve; the two meet at step = warmup = 4000, where the rate peaks at about 0.70e-3 for d_model = 512.
